strengths: High-impact and timely topic: While dynamic text-attributed graphs (DyTAGs) are ubiquitous in real-world applications, generative modeling on them has been substantially bottlenecked by datasets with superficial or missing textual attributes (e.g., DTGB). This benchmark addresses a clear gap in the literature.

Comprehensive dataset suite: The paper curates eight diverse datasets across multiple domains (e-commerce, collaborative networks, social networks, citation networks) encompassing both bipartite and non-bipartite topologies, providing semantically rich text on both nodes and edges.

Well-structured task formulations and multifaceted evaluation: Defining both transductive (TDGG) and inductive (IDGG) settings captures realistic temporal graph expansion. The evaluation protocol thoughtfully assesses topology/spectral fidelity (MMD, power-law), textual quality (five LLM-evaluated criteria), and coupled structural-temporal-textual embeddings (adapted JL-metric).

Extensive empirical study and documentation: The paper benchmarks multiple open-source (DeepSeek-R1-Distill, Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B) and proprietary (GPT-4o-mini) LLMs, performs thorough ablations on memory and reflection mechanisms, analyzes scalability, and provides complete prompt templates in the appendix.
weaknesses: Potentially skewed comparison against DGNN baselines: In the discriminative evaluation under TDGG (Tables 5 and 6), DGNNs are trained on only 1,000 edges (with 8,000 test edges). Conventional DGNNs rely on data-driven parameter updates and inherently struggle in extreme few-shot regimes, whereas LLM-agent backbones leverage vast pre-trained world knowledge. Comparing them primarily under this data-constrained regime should be clearly framed as a few-shot generalization test rather than general superiority over DGNNs.

High computational overhead and scalability limitations of LLM simulation: As shown in the scalability analysis, generating dynamic graphs with LLM multi-agents requires significant runtime (e.g., 16–36 hours for 50k–100k edges). Since real-world dynamic graphs scale to millions of interactions, the practical viability of LLM agent-based generation remains heavily constrained, and the paper would benefit from discussing more lightweight or hybrid generation paradigms.

LLM-as-Evaluator validation: The text evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini scoring. Evaluating text generation with LLMs is susceptible to self-evaluation bias (especially when GPT-4o-mini is also benchmarked as a generator) and verbosity/style biases. Incorporating human correlation checks or cross-evaluator consistency analysis would strengthen the validity of these metrics.

Incremental methodological novelty of GAG-General: While suitable for a benchmark contribution, GAG-General is predominantly an extension of the existing GAG framework (Ji et al., 2025) adapted to general bipartite/non-bipartite graphs with inductive node generation.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap in dynamic graph learning: While dynamic text-attributed graphs (DyTAGs) are prevalent in real-world systems, previous benchmarks primarily focused on discriminative tasks or suffered from minimal/trivial text attributes (e.g., node IDs or email addresses). GDGB introduces eight diverse, meticulously curated datasets with rich textual attributes for both nodes and edges.

Well-formulated generative tasks: The paper clearly formalizes both Transductive Dynamic Graph Generation (TDGG) and Inductive Dynamic Graph Generation (IDGG). The inductive task realistically models open-ended network growth by coupling new node synthesis with edge creation.

Comprehensive, multifaceted evaluation protocol: The evaluation framework holistically captures graph topology (degree/spectral MMD, power-law validation), joint structural-temporal-textual graph embeddings (adapted JL-metric), and qualitative text evaluation across five dimensions.

Extensive experimental benchmarking and ablations: The authors evaluate multiple open-source and closed-source LLMs (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, Llama-3-70B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, and GPT-4o-Mini), ablate the role of node memory and reflection, compare against traditional DGNNs and dynamic graph generators (VRDAG, DG-Gen), and include scalability analyses.

High reproducibility and contribution to the community: Detailed pseudocode, prompt templates across bipartite and non-bipartite domains, and open links to code, datasets, and leaderboards provide a strong foundation for future research.
weaknesses: Potentially unfair baseline setup for DGNNs: In the discriminative evaluation on TDGG (Tables 5 and 6), DGNN baselines are trained on only 1,000 edges and evaluated on 8,000 edges. Parametric DGNNs typically require substantial training interactions to generalize, whereas LLM agent frameworks heavily leverage rich pre-trained representations and world knowledge. Benchmarking DGNNs under extreme data-starved conditions naturally disadvantages them and overstates the advantage of the generative agent paradigm.

Reliance on LLM-as-a-Judge without human calibration: Text quality is evaluated exclusively using GPT-4o-Mini across five qualitative dimensions. Without validation against human annotations or inter-annotator agreement studies, this metric risks model-evaluator bias (especially when evaluating GPT-4o-Mini outputs) and sensitivity to prompt formulation.

Inference latency and computational cost: Generating relatively small graphs (e.g., 10,000 edges in TDGG or 2,000 edges in IDGG) takes 1–2 hours, while generating 50k–100k edges requires 16 to 35+ hours of multi-agent LLM inference. Given that the collected datasets contain millions of edges, the practical applicability of GAG-General to large-scale dynamic graph generation remains computationally constrained.

Scarcity of native DyTAG generative baselines: Because classical continuous-time generative models (VRDAG, DG-Gen) cannot generate text, the comparative IDGG evaluation is restricted to structural and frozen-embedding metrics. While this highlights the novelty of the proposed problem, it limits direct head-to-head competition against existing end-to-end DyTAG generation methods.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and underexplored problem: dynamic text-attributed graph (DyTAG) generation, where existing benchmarks primarily focus on discriminative tasks or lack semantically rich text on both nodes and edges.

The curation of eight diverse datasets across multiple domains (e-commerce, academic citations, social media, biographies) provides a potentially useful resource for future research on dynamic graphs with text attributes.

The paper formalizes two clear generative settings: Transductive Dynamic Graph Generation (TDGG) and Inductive Dynamic Graph Generation (IDGG), moving beyond static one-shot generation toward incremental temporal expansion.
Comprehensive appendix material is provided, including detailed dataset licenses, distributions, prompt templates, and extensive tabular results across multiple LLM backbones.
weaknesses: Fundamentally flawed and unfair experimental comparisons with DGNN baselines: In Section 5.1 and 5.2, dynamic graph neural network baselines (TGN, CAWN, DyGFormer, etc.) are trained on only 1,000 seed edges and evaluated on the subsequent 8,000 edges. Claiming that the LLM agent framework outperforms DGNNs because DGNNs 'exhibit limited capacity and over-reliance on large training input' is misleading. Pre-trained LLMs with tens of billions of parameters inherently possess vast world knowledge, whereas parametric DGNNs trained from scratch on 1,000 edges are severely data-starved. DGNNs should be trained on standard full-scale training splits to provide a realistic upper bound or fair comparison.

Limited technical novelty in the proposed framework: GAG-General is an incremental extension of GAG (Ji et al., 2025), simply applying LLM prompting with memory reflection and candidate selection to non-bipartite topologies. The core generative methodology relies entirely on off-the-shelf LLM agent prompts rather than introducing novel generative modeling principles for dynamic graphs.

Severe computational and scalability limitations: As shown in the scalability analysis, generating just 10,000 edges requires 1.6+ hours, and generating 50,000 edges takes up to 35.7 hours. Given that the curated datasets contain up to millions of interactions, the proposed LLM agent generation paradigm cannot feasibly scale to benchmark realistic graph sizes, heavily restricting its practical utility.

Reliance on LLM-as-Evaluator without human validation: The textual quality evaluation relies on GPT-based scoring across subjective criteria (Personality Depth, Immersive Quality, etc.) on a 1–5 scale. There is no human evaluation or correlation analysis to validate whether the LLM evaluator is reliable, unbiased, or prone to self-preference when evaluating LLM outputs.

Baseline comparisons in IDGG are poorly aligned: VRDAG and DG-Gen are non-textual dynamic graph models that only handle numerical/embedded node/edge vectors. Because they cannot generate text, comparing them on a joint text-structural graph embedding metric where textual features are essentially missing or static is an uneven comparison.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: generative modeling for dynamic text-attributed graphs (DyTAGs), bridging the gap between dynamic graph representation learning and text generation.

Comprehensive benchmark suite comprising eight diverse, meticulously curated DyTAG datasets spanning multiple domains (e-commerce, web interactions, social networks, and citation graphs) with rich node and edge textual descriptions.

Well-formalized task definitions for both Transductive Dynamic Graph Generation (TDGG) and Inductive Dynamic Graph Generation (IDGG), moving beyond static or direct whole-graph generation toward realistic temporal expansion.

Multifaceted evaluation framework that systematically assesses topological fidelity (MMD, power-law validity), textual quality (five-dimensional LLM-as-evaluator and human evaluations), and joint structural-temporal-textual embedding alignment.

Extensive empirical study and thorough documentation, comparing multiple state-of-the-art LLMs, discriminative DGNNs, and dynamic graph generative models, complemented by downstream data augmentation and semantic drift analyses.
weaknesses: The primary proposed generative framework, GAG-General, is largely an adaptation and generalization of the existing GAG multi-agent framework (Ji et al., 2025) to arbitrary topologies and inductive settings via prompt design, rather than a fundamentally new generative architecture.

High computational cost and scalability limitations: Due to the reliance on iterative LLM API queries, the practical benchmarking is conducted on relatively small subsets (e.g., 1,000 seed edges and 2,000–10,000 generated edges), whereas the curated datasets contain up to millions of edges.

Potential evaluation bias in LLM-as-Evaluator: Textual evaluation relies primarily on GPT-4o-Mini scoring, which may favor outputs generated by similar instruction-tuned models or introduce subjective alignment biases, despite the small-scale human check.

The discriminative comparison against conventional DGNNs evaluates models trained on only 1,000 edges; while highlighting low-data performance, dynamic GNNs are typically designed and optimized for larger training regimes, making this comparison somewhat skewed.

strengths: Addresses a timely and significant gap: Dynamic Text-Attributed Graph (DyTAG) research has historically suffered from shallow textual annotations (e.g., node IDs or usernames) and a near-exclusive focus on discriminative tasks. GDGB establishes a much-needed foundation for generative modeling on DyTAGs.

Comprehensive and diverse dataset curation: The benchmark introduces 8 high-quality, text-rich dynamic graph datasets covering multiple domains (e-commerce, web revision, biographies, citation networks, social media) and topological formats (both bipartite and general non-bipartite graphs).

Principled task formulation and multifaceted evaluation: Defining both Transductive Dynamic Graph Generation (TDGG) and Inductive Dynamic Graph Generation (IDGG) effectively separates fixed-node evolution from open-world graph expansion. The evaluation protocol systematically covers structural properties (MMD, power-law validity), semantic fluency/coherence (LLM-as-evaluator, PPL), and joint multi-modal fidelity (extended JL-metric).

Thorough and extensive experimentation: The paper evaluates multiple open- and closed-source LLM backbones (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B, Llama-3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B, GPT-4o-mini), provides insightful ablations on memory and reflection mechanisms, compares against classic dynamic generative baselines (VRDAG, DG-Gen, TIGGER-I) and DGNNs, and validates the downstream utility of generated data for both inductive and transductive tasks.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty of the generative framework: GAG-General is predominantly an engineering adaptation and generalization of the existing GAG framework (Ji et al., 2025) to non-bipartite topologies and unified prompts, rather than a fundamentally new generative paradigm.

Computational overhead and scalability bottlenecks: As highlighted in the scalability experiments, generating larger-scale graphs with LLM multi-agent simulations is computationally heavy (e.g., 100k edges requires ~16 to ~36 hours). While the curated datasets contain hundreds of thousands or millions of interactions, the generative simulation is practical only on small subsets/seeds.

Inherent evaluation bias with LLM-as-Evaluator: Assessing generated text quality using GPT-4o-mini can introduce model-specific stylistic biases, especially when GPT is also evaluated as a generative backbone. Although a human study is included in the appendix, the sample size is relatively modest (50 sampled items).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: bridging generative graph learning with dynamic text-attributed graphs (DyTAGs), moving beyond purely topological or shallow-attribute dynamic graphs.

Curates a solid and diverse collection of 8 high-quality datasets spanning multiple domains (e-commerce, social media, citation networks, celebrity biographies), providing semantically rich raw text for both nodes and edges.

Clearly formalizes two distinct generative tasks: Transductive Dynamic Graph Generation (TDGG) and the more challenging Inductive Dynamic Graph Generation (IDGG) which simulates open-ended real-world network expansion.

Proposes a comprehensive, multifaceted evaluation suite combining structural fidelity (MMD, power-law analysis), intrinsic and LLM-based textual quality, and a unified joint graph embedding metric (extended JL-metric).

Provides extensive experimental validation across four prominent LLM backbones (DeepSeek-R1-Distill, Llama-3, Qwen-2.5, GPT-4o-mini), baseline dynamic generative models (VRDAG, DG-Gen, TIGGER-I), downstream DGNN evaluations, inductive data augmentation tests, semantic drift analysis, and human evaluation.
weaknesses: The core methodological framework, GAG-General, represents primarily an incremental engineering extension of GAG (Ji et al., 2025) to accommodate non-bipartite topologies and unified prompts rather than introducing a fundamentally novel generative learning paradigm.

Scalability remains a bottleneck: due to the high cost of LLM agent simulation, the primary benchmark generations are restricted to relatively small seed graphs (1,000 edges) and target sizes (2,000 to 10,000 edges), leaving a noticeable scale gap with the full multi-million edge datasets provided.

The textual quality metrics heavily rely on an LLM-as-evaluator setup, which may inherit systematic model biases and self-enhancement tendencies toward certain generation styles (though the small-scale human study in the appendix partially addresses this).
